newsitem.title: UK: U.K. shares soar 2.7 pct in pre-Budget rally.
newsitem.headline: U.K. shares soar 2.7 pct in pre-Budget rally.

text.p: The UK's leading stock index scored its biggest one-day gain in point terms for five years on Tuesday, in a pre-Budget rally that caught analysts and dealers by surprise after weeks of cautious trading.

The blue chip FTSE 100 index closed 123.7 points or 2.7 percent higher at 4,728.3, its biggest gain since a rise of 136 points in April 1992 and boosting its value by some 21 billion stg. In percentage terms, the rise was also the biggest since 1992.
Some said the market had looked due for a rally after its recent shaky performance, dogged by worries over the contents of Britain's first Budget under a Labour government in 19 years.
Yet as Wednesday's Budget loomed, there were growing hopes for a tax-raising package to enhance the government's market credibility and prevent the economy overheating.
A fiscal tightening could ease the upward pressure on interest rates that has cast a shadow over shares for months.
"In the short-to-medium term, if they take money out of the economy it's bullish," said the head of equity dealing at one top U.S. investment bank.
"No doubt they are talking about a black hole in public finances to justify a tough budget...I'm not surprised (by the rally) but it has come 48 hours earlier than I expected."

Yet the speed and scale of the rally left many participants struggling for an explanation. Some said market-makers had been caught short of stock ahead of the Budget and had been forced into marking prices sharply higher on relatively thin demand.

"Maybe there is a bit of short-covering ahead of the budget," said another head of equity trading. "There is no particular reason I am aware of but that's the way the market is at the moment, there is not a lot of logic behind it."
Reflecting increased optimism on the inflation and interest rate outlook, gilts also rose. The long gilt future up 23/32 at 114-21/32 and sterling came off recent highs against the mark.
A strong early performance on Wall Street also helped propel UK shares higher.
The Dow was up some 60 points as London trading closed, amid hopes that U.S. rates won't be raised at today's monetary committee meeting.

Yet dealers noted that the FTSE 100's surge had been driven by sharp gains in a relatively small number of stocks -- drug stock Glaxo Wellcome for instance was up 68-1/2p at 13.08-1/2 stg and banking group HSBC Holdings rose 86-1/2p to 19.35 stg.
Overall trading volumes were relatively muted, reaching just 772 million shares by 1644 GMT. Dealers said a sudden sharp rise in the FTSE index future had largely inspired the cash market's advance.
The September future leapt 182 points to,788.0.

Outside the blue chip FTSE 100, gains were less pronounced. The Mid 250 index of second-line stocks rose just 21.2 points or 0.5 percent at 4,452.5 while the FT-A All-Share index, the broadest measure of the UK market, rose 45.91 points or 2.1 percent to 2,230.43.

Dealers said it was no surprise that the broader market continued to languish, even as leading blue chips rampaged higher. They said smaller companies remained prey to a squeeze on margins and sluggish profit growth.
"It's the same old stocks that are driving the market higher, the banks and the pharmaceuticals," said one dealer.
"There are some tremendous moves in a small number of big cap stocks and the rest aren't doing very much."
